groups.title: How impact is counted
groups.explainer: Accounting choices that apply to every charity. Evaluators make these choices differently, and each changes who gets credit for an outcome. The evaluator view uses each evaluator's own choice.

groups.title: Exchange rates between causes
groups.explainer: Every model reports in its own unit: GiveWell's units of value, suffering-adjusted days (SADs) for animals. Animal models counted in other units (animals spared, people reached, research papers) are first converted into SADs. To rank them all on one list, each unit is then converted to GiveWell units of value with the rates below. Change them and the ranking changes; that is the point.

groups.title: Moral weights
groups.explainer: How much good one thing is worth compared to another. These are value judgments, not facts, and they drive most cross-cause comparisons. Defaults follow the evaluator a model was imported from.

groups.title: Economics
groups.explainer: Shared parameters such as how much less a benefit next year counts than one today.

rows.label: Count staff salary sacrifice as a donation
rows.explainer:
Many nonprofit staff earn less than they could in comparable for-profit jobs. That gap is a donation in kind: the staff pay part of the cost of the impact. When this is on, the cost of the work is cash spending plus that forgone salary, so your dollar is credited with only its share of the impact.

When it's off, as in GiveWell's and ACE's models, all of the impact is credited to cash donations. Each model estimates its own staff costs and pay gap, and says how.

rows.label: Give full credit for outcomes shared with other organisations
rows.explainer:
Most outcomes need several organisations: a corporate pledge follows campaigns by several groups. Off (the default, and ACE's approach) credits each charity with its estimated share. On credits each with the whole outcome, on the view that removing any necessary link would have stopped it.

Shares never add up across charities under full credit, so comparisons between charities that share outcomes get harder. Use it to see how much a ranking depends on the choice.

rows.label: Units of value per human DALY averted
rows.explainer:
Bridge from health to GiveWell's units. A rough derivation: GiveWell values an under-five death at 116 units, and a child death in sub-Saharan Africa costs roughly 55–65 years of life, so one year of healthy life is worth about 2 units.

This ignores GiveWell's age weighting and treats years lost to disability like years lost to death. Ours, not GiveWell's.

rows.label: Human DALYs per suffering-adjusted day
rows.explainer:
Suffering-adjusted days (SADs), from Ambitious Impact, count days of animal suffering weighted by pain intensity and by a species' welfare range relative to humans. ACE uses them.

We read one SAD as one human-equivalent day of disabling-level pain and give that day a disability weight of 0.4 (0.1–1.0), so one SAD is 0.4 / 365 DALY. AIM doesn't publish an official SAD-to-DALY rate, so this is the least grounded number on the site and often decides whether animal charities rank above or below global health.

rows.label: Units of value per WELLBY
rows.explainer:
Bridge between the Happier Lives Institute's wellbeing measure and GiveWell's units. HLI estimates GiveDirectly produces 7.55 WELLBYs per $1,000; GiveWell's model gives 8.7 units of value per $1,000. Setting both equal gives about 1.15 units of value per WELLBY, so GiveDirectly scores the same either way.

That calibration assumes the two evaluators measure GiveDirectly's good equally well, which is contested: GiveWell has been sceptical of some WELLBY estimates, HLI of some income-based ones. The wide range is ours.

rows.label: Extra weight on animal suffering, beyond welfare ranges
rows.explainer: SADs already scale suffering by each species' welfare range. At 1 you take those welfare ranges at face value. Below 1 you discount animal suffering further, for example because you're unsure animals are sentient or because you give more weight to humans for other reasons.

rows.label: Suffering-adjusted days per farmed animal spared

source.title: ACE, Dansk Vegetarisk Forening cost-effectiveness sheet (2024)

rows.explainer:
Converts ACE's older headline unit, farmed animals spared from factory farming, into suffering-adjusted days (SADs), so models that count animals spared rank with the rest.

The default is ACE's own ratio for diet change (2024): 2.58 SADs and 0.115 animals spared per meat meal replaced, so about 22 SADs per animal spared. A cross-check from ACE's 2016 models: an animal spared there stands for about 100 days of factory-farmed life, which at Ambitious Impact's 28.9 SADs per year in a battery cage is about 8 SADs.

The range runs from 4, half that cross-check, for mixes of small, short-lived animals, to 45, beyond the ratio of ACE's own bounds (8 to 41). ACE's 2016 models also count welfare reforms as "equivalent animals spared", so the same rate applies to them.

rows.label: Farmed animals spared per person reached by diet-change outreach

source.title: ACE's 2016 Guesstimate models (leaflets, pledges, social media)

rows.explainer:
Converts people reached into animals spared, which then convert into SADs at the rate above. Reach says nothing by itself about behaviour, so this carries the whole judgment about how many people change their diet, by how much and for how long.

ACE's 2016 models give reference points that already allow for people lapsing: about 0.02 animals spared per social media video watched to the end, about 1 per leaflet (ACE later cautioned that the leafleting studies were weak) and about 6 per participant in a week-long vegan pledge. Lapsing is common: Faunalytics (2014) found that about 84% of people who adopt a vegetarian or vegan diet abandon it.

The default weights those reference points by the reach of the one model reported in people reached, Good Food Fund: about 84% of it is online views and online competition entrants, counted like video views, and 16% is people in its cooking network, counted like a leaflet. That gives about 0.18. The range runs from 0.01, below everyone counting as a passing view, to 1.5, everyone counting as more engaged than a leaflet.

rows.label: Suffering-adjusted days per peer-reviewed paper on wild animal welfare
rows.explainer:
**A wide judgment call, not a published estimate.** Research on wild animal welfare does good only through what it later makes possible, and nobody, ACE included, has quantified that. Set this to your own view.

The default is a rough Fermi estimate. Interventions the field enables eventually reach 1 billion wild animals a year (more humane pest control, say), averting 0.5 SADs per animal each year, and arrive 10 years sooner because the field exists. The field succeeds with a 1 in 10 chance, and one paper earns 1/5,000 of its credit. 1 billion × 0.5 × 10 × 0.1 ÷ 5,000 = 100,000 SADs per paper.

Any of those factors could be 10 times higher or lower, so the range runs from 1,000 to 10 million SADs per paper.

rows.label: Value of raising ln(consumption) by 1 for one person for one year
rows.explainer:
GiveWell defines one unit of value as doubling one person's consumption for one year. Doubling raises ln(consumption) by ln 2, so one unit of ln(consumption) is worth 1/ln 2 ≈ 1.44 units.

The low and high ends are the ±25% uniform range GiveWell itself uses in its Monte Carlo inputs. Moving this moves the value of consumption gains relative to deaths averted.

rows.label: Value of saving a life, relative to GiveWell's moral weights
rows.explainer:
GiveWell values averting a child's death at about 116 times the value of doubling one person's consumption for a year, with similar weights for other ages. They come from donor surveys, a survey of people in Ghana and Kenya, and staff judgment.

This multiplies all of GiveWell's life values at once. At 1 you use GiveWell's weights; above 1 saving lives counts for more relative to raising incomes, below 1 for less. The 0.6–1.4 range is ours.

rows.label: Annual discount rate
rows.explainer:
How much less a benefit a year from now counts than one today, compounding. GiveWell and ACE both use 4%.

Used where a model discounts explicitly (ACE's cage-free campaigns). GiveWell's GiveDirectly model has the 4% built into its year 2–10 consumption ratio, so changing this doesn't affect it yet.

uov.label: GiveWell units of value
uov.explainer: One unit = doubling one person's consumption for one year.

sad.label: suffering-adjusted days averted
sad.explainer: Days of animal suffering averted, weighted by pain intensity and species welfare range (Ambitious Impact).

people_reached.label: people reached
people_reached.explainer: People who saw or took part in a diet-change program. Converted into animals spared with the shared rate per person reached, then into SADs.

paper.label: peer-reviewed papers
paper.explainer: Peer-reviewed research papers on wild animal welfare. Converted into SADs with a shared, deliberately wide judgment call about what one paper eventually makes possible.

wellby.label: wellbeing-adjusted life years
wellby.explainer: One point of life satisfaction (0–10) for one person for one year. Used by the Happier Lives Institute.

animals_spared.label: animals spared
animals_spared.explainer: Farmed animals spared from life in factory farming, ACE's 2014–2017 headline unit. It counts animals of every species alike, so it is converted into SADs with the shared rate of SADs per animal spared, then like any SAD.

daly.label: DALYs averted
daly.explainer: Disability-adjusted life years averted. Converted into units of value with the shared DALY exchange rate.
